title: A circle is exactly the conic with A = C and B = 0
statement: For every centre O, every squared radius r2 and every point P, P lies on the conic CPoint.Conic.circle O r2 -- the six-coefficient datum (1, 0, 1, -2 Ox, -2 Oy, Ox^2 + Oy^2 - r2) -- if and only if P lies on the circle of centre O and squared radius r2 in the sense CPoint.OnCircle already had, namely distSq P O ~ r2. The correspondence is an Iff and NOT a definitional identity, and the reason is structural: CPoint.OnCircle compares two quantities while CPoint.OnConic compares one quantity against zero, so moving r2 across the CReal.Equiv is add_right_cancel-shaped work rather than an Eq.refl. The conic's discriminant is CReal.Equiv to -4 with no hypothesis whatever, so every circle is of ellipse type -- including the degenerate r2 <= 0 ones, since being of ellipse type is a statement about the quadratic part A = C = 1, B = 0 and not about the zero set being a nonempty curve.

formal.statement: theorem CPoint.onConic_circle_iff : ((x0 : CPoint) -> ((x1 : CReal) -> ((x2 : CPoint) -> Iff (CPoint.OnConic (CPoint.Conic.circle x0 x1) x2) (CPoint.OnCircle x2 x0 x1))))

evidence.supports: CPoint.onConic_circle_iff is admitted by the trusted kernel gate with the type recorded in formal.statement, and Kernel::axiom_footprint reports 0 assumed names.

notes: WHAT THIS DOES NOT SAY. It does not say the CONVERSE classification -- that a conic with A ~ C and B ~ 0 and a suitable constant term is a circle with some centre and radius. That direction needs completing the square, hence CReal.inv to divide by A, hence a PosBound witness for A, none of which this fact carries. It also does not say the two zero sets are equal as SETS: CPoint has no set former, and the statement is pointwise over a universally quantified P, which is the strongest form available here.
